full_judgment:
2. It is agreed by both the plaintiffs and the defendant that Banizan Bibi was the original owner of the land described in schedule 'A' to the plaint comprising of 0.11 acre. She sold the same to one Sheikh Bishatullah and his brother Sheikh Bagu in 1903. Thereafter the cases of the plaintiffs and the defendant differ. The plaintiffs contend that by amicable partition amongst the co-sharers Bishatullah became the exclusive owner of the entire land. In the year 1920 he verbally sold 0.01 acre of the land to Sheru Bhuiyan. Sheru Bhuiyan died leaving surviving one son Reazuddin as his sole heir. Reazuddin exchanged the said 0.01 acre of land verbally with Shamsuddin. The remaining 0.01 acre was sold by Bishatullah by a registered sale deed dated 13 January 1922 to Abdul Barekt Abdul Mannaf and Abdul Jabbar with full knowledge and consent of Sheikh Bagu who attested the said deed. The purchasers in their turn sold the same to Sirajuddin Bhuiyan and Mokbul Bhuiyan on 18 March 1935. SA Khatian was, however, prepared in the name of Sirajuddin Bhuiyan. Sirajuddin Bhuiyan and Mokbul Bhuiyan constructed their huts on the northern side of the 'A' schedule land covering about 0.06 acre and the remaining 0.05 acre of the land described in schedule 'B' was an open space lying vacant. The plaintiffs are the heirs of Sirajuddin Bhuiyan, Mokbul Bhuiyan and Shamsuddin. They have been owning, possessing and enjoying the entire 'A' schedule land inclusive of the 'B' schedule land. But defendant No. 1 encroached and trespassed upon the disputed 'B' schedule land Hence the suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession in respect thereof. 

 6. The unsuccessful plaintiffs then moved the High Court Division with a revisional application, Civil Revision No. 814 of 1988 and obtained a Rule. After hearing the parties a Division Bench of the said court found that Sheikh Bagu was an attesting witness in the registered sale deed of 1922 (wrongly stated to be the deed of 1935) and that as a prudent man Sheikh Bagu must have noticed in the sale deed which lands were sold to Abdul Barek and others. It was further found that the plaintiffs had produced their kabala and SA Khatian and rent-receipts in the lower appellate Court to show their continuous possession but the said court did not consider the same. With these findings the High Court Division set aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court, but failed to decree the suit in favour of the plaintiffs. Being aggrieved the heirs of defendant No. 1 presented this appeal. 

 11. On the second question it is urged by the learned Counsel for the appellants that the High Court Division has acted beyond its jurisdiction in reversing the concurrent findings of fact of the two courts below disregarding the norms of interference. It cannot be gainsaid that a finding of fact, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court is binding on the High Court, as a revisional court except in certain well-defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of material evidence affecting the merit of the case. In this case it does not appear that there is any such error of law in the findings of the trial Court and the lower appellate Court. It is borne out from the judgment of the lower appellate Court in particular that besides the oral evidence the sale deeds and the SA Khatian on the basis of which the rents were alleged to have been paid by the plaintiffs through rent receipts have been duly considered by the said court which is the final court of fact. We are therefore of the opinion that the learned Judges of the High Court Division were not correct in reversing the concurrent decisions of the courts below.
